result:
The proposed answer of 50 is not supported. The solution never derives it. It guesses a "Möbius strip graph" and attributes the number 50 to "some specific embeddings," which is not a real argument.

I think the exceptional graph is the octahedron, which is planar and 4-regular with 6 vertices and 12 edges. This comes from my recollection of the published result, not from a full proof, so I checked that it is plausible.

- The octahedron has edge connectivity 4. Any cut therefore has at least 4 edges.
- The 1-regular conflict graph is a perfect matching on the 12 edges, which gives 6 conflicting pairs.
- Each pair of adjacent edges meets at one vertex, so a pair can "spoil" the star of at most one vertex. With 6 pairs and 6 vertices, a conflict matching can place one conflicting pair inside the star of every vertex. That blocks all single-vertex cuts.
- Larger cuts, such as a 3+3 split with 9 edges, are also plausible to block with the remaining pairs, so a counterexample is credible.

This points to 6 vertices, not 50.

VERDICT: REJECT
